title: Question 9
stem: Polonium-193 ($^{193}_{84}\text{Po}$) is an unstable nuclide. A nucleus of polonium-193 decays to a nucleus of lead-189 ($^{189}_{82}\text{Pb}$) by emitting an alpha-particle.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem:
Radioactive decay is both random and spontaneous.

State what is meant by:

markscheme_points.text: either: cannot predict when a (particular) nucleus will decay or: cannot predict which nucleus will decay next

hints: Hint 1: Think about a large sample where you can predict the fraction that decays, but focus on one single nucleus - can you know when that one will go?
parts.proper_answer: Random means it cannot be predicted when a particular nucleus will decay, or which nucleus will decay next.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What random really means**
Think of thousands of identical unstable nuclei sitting together. You know very well that on average half will go in one half-life, but for any one labelled nucleus there is no clock ticking inside it. Each nucleus has the same chance of decaying in the next second, and past history makes no difference.

parts.label: (a)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: not affected by external / environmental factors

hints: Hint 1: Imagine heating the sample, squeezing it, or putting it in a magnetic field - ask yourself whether anything outside the nucleus can trigger or stop the decay.
parts.proper_answer: Spontaneous means the decay is not affected by external or environmental factors such as temperature, pressure or chemical state.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What spontaneous really means**
Once a nucleus is unstable, it needs no push, no collision and no energy input to decay. Changing temperature, pressure, chemical bonding or surroundings does nothing to the decay rate. It just happens by itself from inside the nucleus.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on what gets cut in half over a fixed time - is it mass, count of undecayed nuclei, or the rate of decays you would measure?
parts.proper_answer: Half-life is the time taken for the activity of a sample, or the number of undecayed nuclei, to fall to half its initial value.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture halving**
Start with $N_0$ undecayed nuclei and activity $A_0$. After one half-life $t_{1/2}$, on average you have $$\frac{N_0}{2}$$ left and you measure $$\frac{A_0}{2}$$. After another $t_{1/2}$ you have a quarter left, and so on. It is a fixed characteristic time for that nuclide.

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem:
Data for the binding energy per nucleon of the particles involved in the decay of a nucleus of polonium-193 are given in Table 9.1.

Table 9.1
particle | binding energy per nucleon / $\text{eV}$
$^{193}_{84}\text{Po}$ | 7.774
$^{189}_{82}\text{Pb}$ | 7.826
$^{4}_{2}\alpha$ | 7.074
parts.text: Determine the energy, in $\text{eV}$, released when a nucleus of polonium-193 decays into a nucleus of lead-189.
hints: Hint 1: The table gives energy per nucleon, not total energy, so consider how to get the total binding energy for $^{193}$Po, $^{189}$Pb and the alpha-particle from their nucleon numbers.
Hint 2: Think about whether products are more tightly bound than the parent, and how (total of products minus total of parent) gives the released energy.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **From per nucleon to total**
Binding energy per nucleon must be multiplied by the number of nucleons $A$ to get total binding energy. More bound means larger total binding energy, and the extra binding appears as released kinetic energy.

Step 2: **Calculate the difference**
Total binding of products: $$(189 \times 7.826) + (4 \times 7.074) = 1479.1 + 28.30 = 1507.4\text{ eV}$$ Total binding of parent: $$193 \times 7.774 = 1500.4\text{ eV}$$ Energy released: $$E = 1507.4 - 1500.4 \approx 7.0\text{ eV}$$ Positive means the products are more stable and energy is given out.

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.text: State the name of the quantity that is represented by the magnitude of the gradient of the line in Fig. 9.1.
hints: Hint 1: Recall the form $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$ and what happens when you take natural logs - what physical constant appears in front of $t$ as the gradient?
parts.proper_answer: The magnitude of the gradient is the decay constant $\lambda$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link the straight line to the decay equation**
You know $$N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$$ Taking logs: $$\ln\left(\frac{N}{N_0}\right) = -\lambda t$$ This is $y = mx$ with gradient $m = -\lambda$. So the steepness of the $\ln(N/N_0)$ against $t$ graph directly measures $\lambda$, with the minus sign just showing $N$ is falling.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.text: Use Fig. 9.1 to determine the half-life, in $\text{ms}$, of polonium-193.
hints: Hint 1: Pick two widely separated points on the straight line in Fig. 9.1 to find rise over run, remembering to take the positive magnitude and to convert ms correctly.
Hint 2: Once you have the gradient magnitude, think how $t_{1/2}$ is linked to that constant through $\ln 2$ rather than reading directly to $N/N_0 = 1/2$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the gradient magnitude**
Read off a large triangle, for example $\ln(N/N_0)$ falls by $1.4$ in about $0.84\text{ ms}$. So $$\lambda = |\text{gradient}| = \frac{1.4}{0.84\text{ ms}} \approx 1.67\text{ ms}^{-1}$$ Using a big interval keeps the reading error small.

Step 2: **Convert to half-life**
Half-life and decay constant are linked by $$t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$ Hence $$t_{1/2} = \frac{0.693}{1.67\text{ ms}^{-1}} \approx 0.42\text{ ms}$$ This is very short, as expected for the steep fall in Fig. 9.1.

parts.label: (e)(i)
parts.part_stem: Positron emission tomography (PET scanning) uses a radioactive tracer.
parts.text: State what happens to the positrons emitted by the tracer.

markscheme_points.text: positrons collide with electrons and annihilate

hints: Hint 1: Think about what abundant particle inside body tissue a positron will quickly meet, given it is the antiparticle of that particle.
parts.proper_answer: The positrons collide with electrons and annihilate, producing gamma-ray photons.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Fate of the positron**
A positron $\beta^+$ is antimatter. It travels only a few mm in tissue before meeting an ordinary electron. The pair annihilate: mass disappears and two gamma photons fly off in opposite directions, and those gammas are what the PET detectors see.

parts.label: (e)(ii)
parts.text: Explain why a tracer with a half-life of approximately 2 hours is a suitable tracer to use.

markscheme_points.text: long enough to have time to conduct investigation, not so long as to cause patient unnecessary exposure to radiation

hints: Hint 1: Balance two competing needs - the tracer must stay active long enough to take clear images, but not stay active in the patient for days afterwards.
parts.proper_answer: A half-life of about 2 hours is long enough to allow time to carry out the scan, but short enough that the patient is not exposed to unnecessary prolonged radiation.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why hours is just right**
If half-life were seconds, activity would vanish before the tracer reaches the organ and the scanner collects data. If it were years, the patient would keep receiving dose long after the scan. About 2 hours gives a strong signal during the investigation and then decays away quickly, minimising extra dose.
